list.listitem: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is the most common sexually transmitted infection (STI). HPV lives only on squamous epithelial cells. Most infections are asymptomatic and self-limited. B

More than 200 HPV types have been identified to date. These are subdivided into Mucosal type and Cutaneous types. Mucosal types are further divided into high risk oncogenic types (cancer-causing-13 types) and low risk types (anogenital wart (AGW)), which rarely lead to cancer. Oncogenic high-risk HPV types are associated with several cancers, including cervical (90%), vaginal and vulvar (70%), penile, anal, and rectal (60%), and oropharyngeal (60-70%) cancers. Cutaneous types cause common warts in hands arms feets and arms and are not associated with malignancy. B

Primary cervical cancer screening includes the assessment of cervical cytology and detection of oncogenic HPV infection through Pap smear testing. This approach facilitates early detection and helps prevent progression to cervical neoplasia. A

Persistent HPV infection should be considered when clinical evaluation, cervical cytology, histology, or colposcopy results indicate abnormal findings. Cervical biopsy is warranted in the presence of cervical lesions, atypical features, diagnostic uncertainty, or lack of response to therapy. C

Anogenital warts are flesh-colored, exophytic lesions that may be flat, verrucous, or pedunculated. They often present as reddish papules or dome-shaped lesions on keratinized skin. Approximately 90% are caused by non-oncogenic, low-risk HPV types. C
Anogenital warts are typically diagnosed by visual inspection, with biopsy reserved for atypical lesions. Most warts resolve spontaneously, making observation a reasonable management option. C

No single treatment has demonstrated consistent superiority for AGW. Treatment selection depends on physician and patient preferences, available resources, and clinical experience. Most patients require multiple treatment sessions. B
Behavioral interventions that reduce HPV infection or promote HPV clearance include: condom use, A male circumcision, A counseling, B and vaccination.A

HPV vaccines are recommended for males and females at the target age of 11 to 12 years, and are approved for use in individuals aged 9 to 26 years. In 2018, the FDA expanded approval of the 9-valent vaccine to include individuals aged 27 to 45 years. They are not licensed for adults over 45 years old, but can be considered use in those with an increased risk. See for an HPV vaccine schedule.A

Oral HPV is symptomless. Primary transmisson occurs through sexual contact (oral and increased partners), and prevalence ranges from 1-12% in the general population and 20-40% among people living with HIV. It can be identified by testing saliva, and can sometimes persist and can cause throat cancer (oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, OSC) in some people. High risk HPV-16 is the most common type (0.5 -4.7%), and it is 2-3 times more common in men than women with a peak age 51-60 years.

background.definition: Papillomavirus is a double-stranded DNA virus from the Papillomaviridae family that infects a range of species, including birds and humans. Human papillomavirus (HPV) preferentially infects anogenital, oral, and skin epithelium, resulting in benign, precancerous, and malignant lesions. Globally, over 200 HPV genotypes have been identified. Low-risk, non-oncogenic types such as HPV 6 and 11 account for 90% of AGW, while approximately 13 high-risk oncogenic types, primarily HPV16 and 18, are responsible for most precancerous lesions and cancers. HPV is the most common sexually transmitted infection, spread through direct skin-to-skin contact during vaginal, anal, or oral sex with an infected individual. Most HPV infections are self-limiting, but persistent infections can lead to cancers, including cervical, vaginal, and vulvar in women; penile in men; and anal and oropharyngeal in both sexes.

list.listitem: HPV is the most common STI worldwide, with over 13 million new US cases annually.

Globally, annual HPV causes cancer in over 625,000 women and 69,000 men worldwide. High-risk HPV types are linked to many cancers, especially cervical (90%), vaginal/vulvar (70%), penile, anal/rectal (60%), and oropharyngeal (60-70%).
HPV-related cancer rates per 100,000: cervical 15.6, penile 0.92, anorectal 0.55 (men) and 0.75 (women), oropharyngeal 10.6 (men) and 4.8 (women).
The incidence of oncogenic HPV infection was less than 2%. Among men, annual new oral HPV infections occur at 4.4%, with less than 2% for high-risk types..
There are 500,000 to 1 million new anogenital wart (AGW) cases each year (160–289 per 100,000 adults). Incidence peaks before age 24 in women and ages 25–29 in men.
According to the CDC, about 43 million Americans have HPV. High-risk oral HPV affects 4% of adults 18-69, and high-risk genital HPV affects 25% of men and 20% of women.

Globally, the prevalence of HPV varies between genders. In women with normal cervical cytology, the prevalence is >33% in low-income countries and <16% in high-income countries. Prevalence in men is highly variable based on various factors including testing, reporting, sexual trends, and symptoms. In European men, genital HPV DNA prevalence was shown in one study to be 12.4%.
In US women, HPV prevalence dropped from 42.5% to 39.8% between 2003–2006 and 2007–2010, with larger declines in young women for any HPV (32.9% to 26.1%) and vaccine-type HPV (11.5% to 5.1%).
Cervical HPV prevalence is highest in sub-Saharan Africa (24%), followed by Latin America/Caribbean (16%) and both eastern Europe and South-East Asia (14%).
The prevalence of anogenital warts in one study was 0.2–5%, but lifetime risk is higher due to frequent regression.

The prevalence of anogenital warts (AGW) appears to be decreasing among young women aged 15 to 19 years who have been vaccinated. Data from 2014 health care claims among US private health insurance enrollees reflects that among those vaccinated, AGW are decreasing in young women (ages 15–29) and men (ages 20–24); (annual percentage change [APC] = −14.1%; 2008-2014), women aged 20 to 24 years = −12.9%; 2009-2014), women aged 25 to 29 years = −6.0%; 2009-2014), and among men aged 20 to 24 years = −6.5%). In other groups, rates are stable or increasing.
Among sexually active adults, prior to HPV vaccines, about 1 in 100 had AGW at least once in their life time.

In an Australian sexual health center (2002–2013): 4% of men who have sex with men had anal warts, 1.6% had penile warts; 13.7% of heterosexual men had penile warts, and 10% of women had vulvar warts.

Oral HPV overall prevalence ranges from 1-12% in the general population, approximately 5-7%, consistently 2-3 times higher in men than women, and increases with age, peaking in men aged 51-60 years and 20-40% among HIV population. High-risk HPV types, particularly HPV-16, are detected in 0.5-4.7% of individuals, with HPV-16 being the most common type found.

Low-risk HPV types cause non-malignant conditions like common warts, recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, anogenital warts with associated morbidity, and rare but serious complications in immunocompromised individuals.

In immunocompromised people, low-risk HPV can cause severe papillomatosis, including recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), mainly from HPV-6 and HPV-11. RRP is rare but often needs repeated surgery and carries a small cancer risk. Despite being caused by low-risk types, RRP is associated with a 1-3% risk of malignant transformation if not resolved.

Anogenital warts from HPV-6 and HPV-11 affect 1 in 200 young adults. Though benign, they cause discomfort and distress. They are linked to higher anogenital cancer risk, likely due to shared exposure with high-risk HPV or immune issues, not the warts themselves.

HPV-related anal and oropharyngeal cancers are more common in men and at younger ages. Median diagnosis age: cervical 50, vaginal/vulvar/penile 67–69, anal/oropharyngeal 63 (women) and 61 (men). In Scotland, a 2015 cohort study noted 57% of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) cases were HPV-positive, mostly HPV 16 (90%), and better survival among HPV-positive population.

Beta HPV (types 5, 8, 17, 20, 38) usually causes mild cutaneous infections but can raise cutaneous SCC risk, especially in those with weak immune systems and in otherwise healthy individuals (adjusted pooled OR 1.4 [1.2-1.7]).
HPV causes cancer through high-risk HPV integration, E6/E7 oncogene expression, sexual behavior, and immunosuppression.
A study noted that among 161 patients with oropharyngeal cancer, most HPV-associated cases were HPV16 E6-seropositive. Pretreatment HPV16 E6 seropositivity reduced recurrence risk by 86%.

Oral HPV can sometimes persists and can cause oral squamous carcinoma in some people, high risk HPV-16 being the most common type (0.5 -4.7%), 2-3 times higher in men than women, peaks at age 51-60 years of age
HPV screening for cervical cancer provides the same degree of protection over 5 year as a Pap smear does for 3 years, with a similar sensitivity but slightly lower specificity ().A
Self-sampled vaginal HPV DNA screening is acceptable to and preferred by patients over clinician screening.
The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends behavioral counseling for the prevention of STIs for all sexually active adolescents and adults at increased risk. B

HPV vaccines are recommended for females and males at the target age of 11 to 12 years, and are approved for use in individuals aged 9 to 45 years. They are not licensed for adults over 45 years old, but can be considered for use in those with an increased risk. See for the vaccine schedule. A

The chapter on "Cervical cancer screening and Pap smears" and guidelines from ASCCP.com and the USPSTF recommendation statements provide detailed discussion of screening for cervical cancer in women (). A

HPV is divided into Mucosal type and Cutaneous types. Mucosal types are further divided into high risk oncogenic types (cancer-causing-13 types) and low risk types (anogenital wart (AGW)), which rarely lead to cancer. Oncogenic high-risk HPV types are associated with several cancers, including cervical (90%), vaginal and vulvar (70%), penile, anal, and rectal (60%), and oropharyngeal (60-70%) cancers. Cutaneous types cause common warts in hands arms feets and arms and are not associated with malignancy. The purpose of screening is to detect the high-risk oncogenic types. See .

There is growing emphasis on using HPV testing alone as primary testing for cervical neoplasia. A negative HPV test provides the same degree of protection over 5 years as a negative cytology by Pap smear does for 3 years, with a similar sensitivity but slightly lower specificity.

Several studies show that self-sampled HPV tests have potentially similar diagnostic capabilities as clinician-sampled HPV tests and can provide greater statisfaction as well as being more cost effective. Self-sampled vaginal HPV DNA screening is acceptable to and preferred by patients over clinician screening. Self sampling HPV kits are available in United States.
Based on a trial conducted in the Netherlands, extension of the cervical screening interval beyond 5 years may be justified for women aged 40 years and older who are HPV negative.
Currently there are no screening guidelines on HPV infection in males or for screening for anogential warts.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of two rapid HPV DNA assays, careHPV and OncoE6, found the former had good sensitivity and specificity for the detection of histological cervical intra epithelial neoplasia (CIN) 2+ using cervical samples for cervical cancer screening (88 and 84%, respectively). Sensitivity and specificity were similarly high for CIN3+. The pooled prevalences for CIN2+ and CIN3+ were 2.3% and 1.1%, respectively, of 29,657 women screened.
See the chapter on "Cervical cancer screening and Pap smears" for a more detailed discussion of screening in women.
HPV DNA in the oral cavity, typically detected through oral rinse or gargle samples, usually asymptomatic and no efective screening guidelines.

Behavioral interventions like condom use, male circumcision, counseling, and vaccination can reduce HPV infection or promote clearance. Risk-reduction counseling at the time of rapid HIV testing among adults does not reduce the risk of subsequent STIs.

The USPSTF recommends behavioral counseling for the prevention of STIs for all sexually active adolescents and adults at increased risk. Risk factors include history of an STI within the past year, inconsistent condom use, multiple sex partners, or a partner at high risk for STIs. Group or individual counseling lasting more than 2 hours was associated with larger reductions in STI incidence, interventions of <30 minutes are also likely effective.

Condoms reduce the risk of acquiring HPV, prevent other STIs and are associated with increased rates of clearance of cervical HPV lesions. Consistent condom use reduced new HPV infections by about 70% and a 35% reduction in HPV persistence (infection lasting more than six months). Behavioral interventions targeting young women are effective for encouraging condom use but not for abstaining from or reducing sexual activity.

Consistent condom use helps reduce HPV infection and anogential warts, but does not fully protect uncovered areas. Evidence for wart prevention is mixed due to skin to skin transmision and viral particles on the surface.

Oral HPV spreads mainly through oral sex, but can be passed by deep kissing, shared items, or through vertical transmission. Most infections clear in 1–2 years spontaneously. If a high-risk types like HPV-16 persists, the throat cancer risk increases.

HPV vaccination is a critical prevention tool against HPV infection, anogenital warts, and HPV-attributable precancers and cancers. It has also been shown to reduced the likelihood of invasive cervical cancer (adjusted incidence rate ratio [a[RR] 0.4; 95% CI 0.2 - 0.6), especially if vaccinated before age 17 years (a[RR] 0.12; 95% CI 0.0 - 0.3).

WHO’s 2022 position paper emphasizes HPV vaccination starting at age 9 and aims for 90% global coverage by 2030. Globally available vaccines include bivalent (2–valent- 6,11), quadrivalent (4–valent- 6,11,16,18) and Nonavalent (9–valent- targets HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58).

HPV vaccine is recommended by the US Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices for prevention of cervical, vulvar, vaginal, anal, oropharyngeal, and other head and neck cancers, anogenital precancerous and dysplastic lesions, and AGW in females and for prevention of anal, oropharyngeal, and other head and neck cancers, anal precancerous and dysplastic lesions, and AGW in males.

HPV vaccines 9-valent vaccine are recommended for boys and girls at target age 9-11 years, but are approved for males and females age 9-26 years and extended to individuals age 27-45 years. See for the recommended HPV vaccine schedule.

The vaccine can be given in a two-dose regimen for those less than age 15 years, with the second dose given 6-12 months after the first dose. The three-dose regimen is recommended for those who are over the age of 15 at 0, 1-2 and 6 months duration. In case of delayed administration of the second or third dose, the series dose does not need to be restarted and there is no current indication for a booster vaccine.
Immunocompromised individuals (HIV) should undergo the three-dose regimen of the 9-valent vaccine.
HPV vaccination is not associated with earlier onset of sexual activity or with increased incidence of STIs

Following HPV vaccination, seroconversion rates are 93 to 100 percent in females and 99 to 100 percent in males. The HPV vaccine can prevent 92% of HPV-attributable cancers in the future. HPV vaccine efficacy is 97% (95% CI, 80.9%-100%) for preventing HPV 16- or 18-related cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) based on phase III clinical studies in the HPV-naive population. The vaccine is less effective in previously exposed females.

A Scottish study among of 138,693 women found that cervical cancer risk was much lower in women who received all 3 doses of the HPV vaccine (0.06%) compared to those unvaccinated (0.59%). 189 women need to be vaccinated to prevent one serious case.

HPV vaccine side effects are rare [combined analysis of 7 phase III clinical trials as 0.1% and <0.1%, respectively]. Serious reactions occur in less than 0.1%; injection site discomfort is most common. There’s no known link to chronic fatigue or other autonomic dysfunctional syndromes. With 135 million doses given in the US, the vaccine is safe and effective..

The vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy; however, safety data regarding inadvertent administration of the vaccine during pregnancy has been reassuring. If a patient becomes pregnant, the vaccine series should be completed after pregnancy is competed. The vaccine can be given during breastfeeding.
Circumcision in men reduces the likelihood of HPV infection (aOR 0.37).

Authors of a systematic review found that many practice and community-based interventions, including reminder and recall systems, physician-focused interventions such as audit and feedback, school-based programs, and social marketing, can increase HPV vaccination rates. Increasing HPV vaccine knowledge alone does not translate into increased vaccine uptake or completion. A cohort study, identified by continuing the conversation with hesitant parents to vaccinate their adolescents against HPV for a median of 1 additional minute resulted in same-day vaccination in 51% of adolescents.C
HPV vaccination helps to reduce recurrence and disease burden in most studies when used as an extra treatment for active disease, but showed no benefit in people with HPV but no symptoms.
Secondary prevention measures are summarized in
Vaccination against HPV-16 and HPV-18 reduces incident and persistent infections with efficacy of 91.6% (95% confidence interval [CI], 64.5%–98.0%) and 100% (95% CI, 45%–100%), respectively.

In men, the vaccine is about 47% (95% CI 28.6-60.8%) effective against persistent HPV 16 genital infections and 88% against persistent oral infections [systematic review of 4 RCTs and 3 nonrandomized studies]

HPV infection should be suspected based on clinical evaluation of the lesions, cytology, histology and colposcopy results. Anogenital warts caused by HPV are flesh-colored, exophytic lesions called as condyloma accuminta. They may be flat, verrucous, or pedunculated, and may appear as reddish papules or dome-shaped lesions on keratinized skin. C

Diagnosis of anogenital warts is clinical; biopsy if atypical features are noted like bleeding, ulceration, pigmentation, palpable dermal infiltration, not responding to therapy as expected, or in patients with persistent warts, especially if immunocompromised. Biopsy cervical lesions in women when the diagnosis is uncertain.C

Diagnosis of HPV infection is confirmed by nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) to detect the 13 high-risk HPV types. Two NAAT tests are available to specifically detect HPV genotypes 16 or 18. C

Colposcopy with or without biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) caused by HPV infection. Appropriate clinical uses of high-risk HPV testing include co-testing with cervical cytology screening in women aged 30 years or older, triage or surveillance of certain abnormal cytology results, and post treatment surveillance. C
No established screening program for oral HPV infection or oropharyngeal cancer (OCP) in asymptomatic individuals, and the USPSTF do not recommend routine screening. A
HPV infection should be suspected based on clinical evaluation of the lesions, cytology, histology and colposcopy results.

Cutaneous warts, the reliable diagnostic features include the presence of black dots (capillary thrombosis), showed the highest interobserver agreement in validation studies, along with hyperkeratotic appearance, flesh-colored lesions with discrete margins. Diagnosis is typically made by observing flesh-colored, exophytic lesions on the cutaneous regions. Warts may be flat, verrucous, or pedunculated and appear as reddish papules or dome-shaped lesions on keratinized skin. Common sites include the hands, elbows, knees, and feet. According to one large study, only about a quarter of women infected with HPV 6 or 11 actually developed genital warts.

For anogenital warts, diagnosis is made by clinical appearance and history. Genital warts are primarily noted on the penis, vulva, scrotum, perineum, and perianal skin. Less commonly warts may be seen on the vaginal or cervical mucosa, the urethra, the anus, or the mouth. It is important to examine the urethral meatus and perianal area. Consider using speculum exam for cervical and vaginal lesions proctoscopy or anoscopy to examine the intra anal lesions. Anogenital warts are flesh-colored, exophytic lesions called as condyloma accuminta. They may be flat, verrucous, or pedunculated, and may appear as reddish papules or dome-shaped lesions on keratinized skin

Women are asymptomatic secondary to HPV infecion. Prolonged hr HPV infection progress to cervical cancer. Abnormal bleeding, spotting, watery vaginal discharge, or post coital bleeding are common symptoms. CIN and Carcinoma in situ (CIS) caused by HPV infection are can be visualized through colposcopy examination of the cervix and confirmed by cervical biopsy if suspicious lesion identified.

Diagnosis of anogenital warts is clinical; biopsy if atypical features are noted like bleeding, ulceration, pigmentation, palpable dermal infiltration, not responding to therapy as expected, or in patients with persistent warts, especially if immunocompromised. Biopsy cervical lesions in women when the diagnosis is uncertain.
Diagnosis of HPV infection is confirmed by nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) to detect the 13 high-risk HPV types. Two NAAT tests are available to specifically detect HPV genotypes 16 or 18.

HPV testing is unuseful and not recommended for wart diagnosis, as results are not confirmatory and do not guide management. Typical AGW do not require diagnostic testing by biopsy or HPV serotyping as the diagnosis is by clinical evaluation.

Biopsy is recommended for exophytic warts on the cervix to exclude dysplasia or cancer. Biopsy of the lesions is recommended for definitive diagnosis include those in whom the diagnosis is unclear, immunocompromised patients, patients not responding to or worsening during appropriate therapy, and patients with warts that are pigmented, indurated, fixed, or ulcerated. Also, patients at high risk for HPV-related malignancy (eg, chronic genital warts, history of abnormal Pap smear) should have definitive testing to confirm the diagnosis.

Colposcopy with or without biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) caused by HPV infection. Diagnosis of HPV infection most commonly results from routine cervical PAP screening methods.

With respect to oral pharyngeal cancers (OCP), HPV16 E6 serum antibodies have potential clinical utility for diagnosis and prognosis of HPV-OPC,. Diagnosed OCP, the NCCN guidelines require p16 immunohistochemistry testing to determine HPV status, for prognosis and treatment decisions.

Diagnosis is usually made on clinical grounds by visual inspection or by routine screening. Typical anogenital warts do not require diagnostic testing by biopsy or HPV typing. Offer STI screening to patient and partner. Positive screening tests require follow up diagnostic colposcopy with or without biopsy.

Topical therapies (both patient and physician administered) have high failure and recurrence rates. Surgical therapies (electrosurgery, scissors excision) have the best clearance rates, but still have moderately high recurrence rates.

Primary prevention by vaccination, screen all adults for tobacco use, recommend against tobacco use, provide tobacco cessation interventions for those who use tobacco products and behavioral counseling interventions in primary care settings to reduce alcohol misuse by adults.
Primary screening by cervical cytology, and with HPV co testing screening. Colposcopy with or without biopsy is the gold standard for CIN caused by HPV infection.
The USPSTF does not recommend screening for oral cancer or oropharyngeal cancer in asymptomatic adults by primary care physicians.
No individual treatment has been shown consistently better than another—treatment selection is based on physician and patient preferences, resources, and experience. B
Most warts resolve spontaneously, and observation alone is a viable option. C
Most patients require multiple treatments to treat genital warts rather than a single treatment. B
Colposcopy with or without biopsy is the gold standard for CIN caused by HPV infection.
Latent or productive HPV infection can be managed by observation or excision according to ASCCP guidelines. B
Treatment of neoplastic HPV infection requires excision of the lesion. A

Vaccination is the current recommendations for PRIMARY HPV prevention. HPV vaccination: Two-dose series for ages 9 to 14 years. Three-dose series for ages 15 to 26 years and for ages 27 to 45 years through shared decision-making. No recommendation to administer the vaccine in patients older than 45 years. A

Treatment of subclinical HPV (no visible warts or squamous intraepithelial lesions on Pap test) does not change the course of the disease and is not recommended. The goal of treatment is to improve symptoms or remove visible warts; treatment does not eradicate HPV infection. Lesions may resolve spontaneously, and "watchful waiting" is a reasonable treatment option. Topical treatment can be patient or clinician applied.

Patient application: Patient-applied options include podofilox 0.5% solution or 0.15% cream, imiquimod cream 3.75% and 5% and sinecatechins ointment 15%. Podofilox 0.5% solution may be administered at home and is associated with an 84% probability of complete clearance of genital warts at the end of treatment. Although self-administered, imiquimod and sinecatechins are less effective. TCA is administered by a physician.
A biologically active extract of podophyllin, which can be self-applied twice daily for 3 days consecutively for a week; may repeat for 4 cycles. Clearance rates range from 54% to 77%.

An immunomodulatory cream that induces macrophages to secrete cytokines such as interferon-gamma, which in turn stimulates a cell-mediated response against HPV. It is applied 3 times weekly for up to 8 to 16 weeks.
Ointment is a water extract of green tea leaves that decreases viral replication through apoptosis and proinflammatory response. It can be applied three times a day for up to 16 weeks.
Topicals are left in place for a specified number of hours and washed off with soap and water.
Clinician applied options include podophyllin 25%, trichlorocetic acid/bichlorocetic acid (TCA/BCA) and interferon.

Podophyllin is an antimitotic agent that disrupts viral activity by inducing local tissue necrosis. It is applied to each wart weekly for a maximum for four weeks. Not a first-line treatment due to risk of systemic toxicity if used incorrectly.
TCA/BCA are proteolytic agents that are applied to warts and can be reapplied weekly as needed for removal. Clearance rates range from 64%-88%.
Interferon is an intralesion injection that is effective for removal; however, it is not recommended as first-line treatment.

Imiquimod (Aldara) was more effective than placebo in two small clinical trials including one randomized trial with 52 patients. Two RCTs in patients with HIV and anogenital warts or high-grade anal intraepithelial neoplasia (IEN) failed to show significant differences in complete clearance or progression with imiquimod 5% cream. Electrocautery appears to have some advantage in the treatment of intra-anal IEN in patients with HIV over imiquimod, but there were no significant differences in perineal IEN and numbers of participants in all these trials are small.
A randomized trial with 326 patients compared podofilox gel with placebo and found better clearance rates at 8 weeks with active treatment (45% vs. 4%, NNT = 2).

A European guideline based on a systematic literature reviewed reported the following intention to treat clearance rates: podophyllotoxin solution or cream 43% to 83%, imiquimod 5% cream 35% to 68%, sinecatechins from green tea extract 47% to 59%, cryotherapy 44% to 75%, and trichloracetic acid 55% to 81%. Recurrence rates were generally in the range of 20% to 40%.

In an RCT of 90 women diagnosed with subclinical or latent HPV infection of the vagina and cervix, HPV clearance rates and infection cure rates were higher using either high-dose interferon α-2b (9 million IU) alone or high-dose interferon α-2b and red light therapy compared to low-dose interferon (1 million IU) alone immediately and 4, 8, and 12 weeks after treatment. HPV clearance rates were 68.8% (95% confidence interval [CI] 52.2%-85.3%), 86.5% (95% CI 74.3%-98.8%) and 27.1% (95% CI 11.2%-43%), respectively. Subclinical and latent infection cure rates were 63.3% (95% CI 46.1%-80.6%) 83.3% (95% CI 70%-96.7%) and 20% (95% CI 5.7%-34.3%), respectively.
Longer courses of treatment may be needed in immunocompromised patients and those with HIV infections. There are no drug treatment options for intravaginal or cervical HPV.

Topical 5 fluorouracil (5-FU) works by stopping DNA production of the virus. Authors of a Cochrane database systematic review concluded that 5-FU more effective than placebo or no treatment. There is lack of RCTs and further studies are needed.
Primary screening by cervical cytology, and with HPV co testing screening. Colposcopy with or without biopsy is the gold standard for CIN caused by HPV infection.
Latent or productive HPV infection can be managed by observation or excision according to ASCCP guidelines.B
Warts and AGW lesions can be destroyed by excision, cryotherapy or laser ablation.
Treatment of oropharyngeal cancer due to oral neoplastic HPV infection requires excision of the lesion.

Uses liquid nitrogen or cryoprobe applied directly to the wart and 2 mm surrounding the lesion to cause tissue damage and cell death; may repeat applications every 1 to 2 weeks if necessary. Recommended for external genital, vaginal, anal, cervical and urethral meatus warts. Clears within less than 3 treatments with a clearance rate of 44% to 75%, with decreased efficacy in patients >40 years of age. First-line treatmen for pregnant women
A beam of infrared light energy used to vaporize anaogenital warts; treatment of choice for immunocompromised and pregnant patients not responding to cryotherapy.

Studies show that combination therapies including surgical therapy and drug therapy are more effective than single methods alone. One single-blind RCT showed that cryotherapy plus sinecatechins 15% ointment was more effective in treatment of anogenital warts than cryotherapy alone.
In patients with respiratory papillomatosis, surgical debulking is the usual therapy.
Sinecatechin polyphenon E ointment is a botanical green tea extract shown to be effective as a topical therapy for anogenital warts based on a systematic revie.

Complications of treatment are unusual. Based on very limited data, minor local side effects like hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation are relatively common, hypertrophic or depressed scars are uncommon and chronic pain is rare.
Confine treatments to affected areas to limit complications.

Spontaneous regression of cutaneous and anogenital warts (AGW) is thought to be relatively common but exact regression rates have not been consistently reported. Recurrence is common at approximately 30%. Approximately 30% of AGW resolve spontaneously within 4 months, and in pediatric populations, almost 90% clear within two years. If left untreated, AGW can resolve spontaneously, remain unchanged, or increase in size or number.C

Malignant transformation is rare, as AGW are caused by nononcogenic HPV types 6 or 11 in 90% of cases. Squamous cell carcinomas arising in or resembling AGW might occur among immunosuppressed persons.
The psychosocial impact can be significant, with anogenital warts associated with increased anxiety and depression and substantial negative impact on personal relationships.

Persistant HPV: Among 10,860 women aged 30 and older who tested positive for high-risk HPV on one of two assays but had negative baseline cytology and histology for CIN 2+ on colposcopy, 6.3% and 5.1% developed CIN 2+ within 3 years. In contrast, less than 0.3% of women negative on both assays developed CIN 2+. A 13-year follow-up of 195 women who were cytologically normal with persistent HPV positive for at least 12 months found that, among 75 women, 35 cleared HPV and 40 had HPV persistence. Women who cleared HPV did not develop severe cervical disease (CIN2+ or worse). Womenl with persistent infection and over half with unknown status (56%) did develop CIN or worse—most within 6 years. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found that natural HPV infection gives only modest protection against future cervical HPV in women (RR ~0.65–0.70), and offers no immunity for men.
In the population study of oral HPV in men, just over half cleared spontaneously in a median time of 6.9 months (95% CI, 6.2-9.3 months).
AGW / Warts: Follow-up examination 3 months after successful treatment may be helpful, patients may be unable to see residual AGW and cutaneous warts after treatment.
For HPV-related cervical changes, monitoring and treatment strategies should be followed according to the ASCCP guidelines.

Treatment of HPV infection in pregnancy focuses on managing visible AGWs and precancerous lesions, as there is no specific antiviral therapy to eradicate the virus itself and the treatment resolution might be incomplete until after delivery.

Treatment for AGW and warts during pregnancy may prevent further proliferation or friability. TCA is the treatment of choice and ablative treatment methods (cryotherapy/laser or excision) may be used. Imiquimod, podophyllin, and podofilox should not be used during pregnancy.

For cervical abnormalities, colposcopy and cervical biopsy can be performed during pregnancy forr high-grade disease lesions or suspicious of cancer, low-grade lesions (ASC-US or LSIL) can be deferred until at least 6 weeks postpartum. ECC and treatment of CIN is not recommended during pregnancy unless invasive disease is suspected.

Cesarean section should not be performed solely to prevent transmission of HPV to the newborn but women with visible genital warts should be advised concerning the low risk for warts in the infant's larynx (respiratory papillomatosis).

Treatment outcomes are not different in HIV-infected patients and treatment modality selection is the same; however, patients may have larger or more numerous warts, or may not respond as well. Cesarean section may be indicated for women with larger warts that would impair vaginal delivery.
Treatment of HPV infection in children and adolescents focuses on managing AGW and warts by preventing infection through vaccination, as there is no antiviral therapy to eradicate the virus itself.

For anogenital warts in preadolescent children, an initial wait-and-see approach is often appropriate, as spontaneous clearing occurs in almost 90% of cases within two years in asymptomatic immunocompetent children.
For persistent or symptomatic lesions, topical therapies are preferred due to their low aggressiveness and manageability in children

Imiquimod 5% cream - moderately effective with tolerable side effects limited to mild irritation and erythema. Sinecatechins 15% ointment - shows a trend toward greater effectiveness than imiquimod, with 8 out of 9 patients responding (5 complete, 3 partial responses) Podophyllotoxin (podofilox) 0.5% solution or 5% gel - reported to be safe and efficacious.
Cryotherapy, TCA, BCA, laser therapy, and surgical excision are options based on wart characteristics, patient preference, and provider experience.

*If the second dose was administered less than five months after the first, the dose should be repeated a minimum of 12 weeks after the second dose and a minimum of five months after the first.For the 2-dose schedule, the second shot should be given 6–12 months after the first shot. If the second shot is given less than 5 months after the first shot, a third shot should be given at least 4 months after the second shot. For the 3-dose schedule, the second shot should be given 2 months after the first shot and the third shot should be given 6 months after the first shot.

**Immunocompromised patients: B-lymphocyte antibody deficiencies, complete or partial T-lymphocyte defects, HIV infection, malignant neoplasm, transplantation, autoimmune disease, and immunosuppressive therapy.
